facts.text: The black-chinned honeyeater is a mid-sized honeyeater with olive-brown upperparts, a buff underside and a black head and throat.
facts.quote: A mid-sized honeyeater ranging from 14 to 16 cm (5.6–6.4 in) in length, it is olive-brown above and buff below, with a black head, nape and throat

facts.text: It has a striking bluish patch of bare skin over the eye and a white crescent-shaped patch on the nape.
facts.quote: with a bluish patch of bare skin over the eye and a white crescent-shaped patch on the nape

facts.text: It makes a scratchy creep-creep-creep call as well as a more musical one.
facts.quote: It makes a scratchy creep-creep-creep call, as well as a more musical one.

facts.text: It forages by probing into the bark of tree trunks and branches, like its close relatives the brown-headed and strong-billed honeyeaters.
facts.quote: like its close relatives, the brown-headed and strong-billed honeyeaters, the black-chinned honeyeater forages by probing in the bark of trunks and branches of trees.

facts.text: It may nest from July to December, breeding once or twice in that period.
facts.quote: Black-chinned honeyeaters may nest from July to December, breeding once or twice during this time.

facts.text: Its nest is a thick-walled bowl of grasses and bark, hidden in the outer foliage of a tall tree, usually a eucalypt.
facts.quote: The nest is a thick-walled bowl of grasses and bits of bark, lined with softer plant material, hidden in the outer foliage of a tall tree, usually a eucalypt.

facts.text: It usually lays two shiny, buff-pink eggs sparsely spotted with red-brown.
facts.quote: One or (more commonly) two eggs are laid, 22 × 16 mm in size, and shiny, buff-pink, sparsely spotted with red-brown

facts.text: It lives in open woodland and dry sclerophyll forest, often near watercourses.
facts.quote: It lives in open woodland and dry sclerophyll forest, often near watercourses.
